cases.question: When do agents get selfish as resources become scarce?

output.explanation: The commons environment supports a controlled test of whether scarce endowments reduce the fraction contributed. Here, 'selfishness' means lower proportional contributions, not an inferred motive. Two resource levels test a scarcity effect but cannot identify an exact threshold.

design.title: Cooperation under resource scarcity
design.question: Do model-controlled agents contribute a smaller fraction of their available resources when endowments fall from 20 to 5, and how does this difference vary over 12 rounds?
design.hypothesis: Agents with endowments of 5 will contribute a smaller fraction of available resources than otherwise identical agents with endowments of 20.
design.context: Six model-controlled agents make sealed contributions and receive shared returns, with communication and public commitments available. Operationalize increased selfishness as a lower contribution rate under scarcity, not merely fewer units contributed. Compare each run's mean contribution rate across matched seeds; inspect round-by-round differences descriptively. Conditions have fixed endowments throughout, rather than a resource decline within a run. All profiles are experimental goal specifications, not validated representations of humans.

cases.question: Does allowing communication improve cooperation?

output.explanation: Test communication in a controlled commons study, defining cooperation as the fraction of available resources contributed. Matched conditions differ only in communication availability; results describe model-controlled agents, not validated human behavior.

design.title: Does communication improve cooperation in a commons?
design.question: Does enabling communication increase model-controlled agents' mean contribution rate in a repeated commons game?
design.hypothesis: Communication-enabled groups will have a higher mean contribution rate than otherwise identical groups without communication.
design.context: Six model-controlled agents make sealed contributions and receive shared returns over 12 rounds. Cooperation is operationalized as contribution_rate, not inferred intent. Compare each condition's mean contribution rate across rounds within each matched seed, then summarize the paired differences across seeds, including their variability. A positive difference supports the hypothesis in this setting; mixed or near-zero differences remain inconclusive. Group payoff is a secondary outcome. Profiles specify experimental goals, not validated human types.

cases.question: Who keeps their promises under pressure?

output.explanation: This can be studied as observable promise-keeping by model-controlled agents using public commitments and sealed contributions. Lower endowments operationalize resource pressure; results would not identify trustworthy humans or establish stable personality traits.

design.title: Who keeps public commitments under resource pressure?
design.question: Which model-controlled agents fulfill their public contribution commitments, and does reducing available resources change promise fulfillment?
design.hypothesis: Lower endowments may reduce promise fulfillment, although agents could instead adapt by making smaller commitments. Differences among identical agent profiles are exploratory, not evidence of stable character.
design.context: Six model-controlled participants play a repeated commons game with public commitments and sealed contributions. Operationalize pressure solely as a lower per-round endowment. Evaluate promise keeping using promise_fulfillment_rate: whether actual contributions meet public contribution commitments. Interpret fulfillment conditional on an evaluable commitment; absence of a commitment is not evidence of keeping one. Consider contribution_rate alongside fulfillment to distinguish keeping modest commitments from contributing generously. Compare conditions within matched seeds, treating each seed's six-agent group as the independent unit. Any per-agent descriptions of who kept promises are exploratory and limited to these runs; agent names do not represent validated human types.

cases.question: Do agents return trust or exploit generous partners?

output.explanation: A repeated trust-exchange study can measure transfers and returns. Partner-goal prompts can encourage generosity without forcing it; observed transfer rates must confirm whether generosity actually increases. This tests model behavior, not human trust or motives.

design.title: Reciprocation when partners are encouraged toward generosity
design.question: Do model-controlled agents reciprocate transfers from partners whose goals emphasize shared payoff, or show low returns despite generous transfers?
design.hypothesis: Emphasizing shared payoff in partner goals will increase trust_rate. If that generosity is reciprocated, return_rate will also rise; increased trust_rate without increased return_rate is consistent with unreciprocated generosity.
design.context: Use the environment's repeated paired transfers and existing pairing rules. Alex, Morgan and Sam are focal agents with unchanged goals. Jordan, Casey and Taylor receive the partner-goal intervention. Roles label study groups; they do not alter pairing rules. Compare conditions within matched seeds. Check trust_rate first to establish whether the encouragement increased transfers, then compare return_rate. Use participant or pair attribution only if exposed by the environment; otherwise interpret results at group level. High transfers accompanied by low returns operationalize unreciprocated generosity, not deliberate exploitation. No forced transfers, new payoff rules or controlled pairing are assumed.

cases.question: Which strategy earns the most while preserving group welfare?

output.explanation: A controlled commons study can compare the earnings of two prompted strategies while measuring group welfare. It cannot establish a universally optimal strategy or predict human behavior; the winner must be determined from observed results.

design.title: Personal earnings subject to a group-welfare floor
design.question: Among stable and history-responsive contribution strategies, which gives a focal model-controlled agent the highest cumulative payoff while maintaining at least 90% of the group's maximum achievable total payoff?
design.hypothesis: History-responsive contribution planning may improve focal earnings relative to stable planning, but it may also reduce group welfare enough to fail the welfare criterion.
design.context: Six model-controlled agents participate in a repeated commons with sealed contributions and shared returns. Alex is the focal agent; the other five agents have identical goals across conditions. Compare prompted contribution-planning strategies, not enforced algorithms. With six agents, endowment 10, multiplier 2 and 12 rounds, full contribution yields a group-payoff benchmark of 1440. Define welfare preservation as cumulative group payoff of at least 1296, including Alex. For each seed, record Alex's cumulative payoff and whether the group passes this floor. A strategy is provisionally eligible only if it passes in every sampled seed; rank eligible strategies by mean focal payoff using matched-seed differences. Report each seed's results and uncertainty. If neither qualifies, report no qualifying strategy; if differences are inconclusive, report no clear winner. These criteria are analysis rules, not enforced contribution constraints or bargaining agreements.

cases.question: Do agents adapt when their partners stop cooperating?
cases.capability_gap: A goal schedule can explore changing priorities, but cannot force a partner-policy switch. Any supported proxy must disclose that limit and check the realized behavior.

output.explanation: This can be studied as observable adjustment in a repeated commons game. Partner goal text can change after the midpoint, but the available mechanics cannot force partners to stop cooperating. The study therefore checks whether partner contributions actually decline before assessing focal agents' responses.

design.title: Adjustment after partners reduce cooperation
design.question: Do model-controlled agents adjust their contributions after partners with changed payoff priorities reduce their contributions?
design.hypothesis: If partner contributions decline after their goal priorities change, focal agents will subsequently reduce their own contribution rates relative to the stable-goal control. Continued cooperation or increased contributions are alternative observable responses.
design.context: Run six agents for 12 rounds. Alex, Morgan and Sam are focal agents; Jordan, Casey and Taylor are the partner subgroup. These labels do not add roles or powers to the commons rules. Conditions differ only in partner private-goal text concerning rounds 7–12. Round-dependent priorities are prompt instructions, not an enforced action schedule. First compare partner contribution rates in rounds 1–6 versus 7–12 across matched conditions. Only interpret responses as adjustment to reduced cooperation if partner contributions actually fall more in the changed-priority condition. Examine focal contribution rates over subsequent rounds, comparing their pre/post change with the control. Separate immediate round-7 changes from later responses because sealed simultaneous contributions cannot reveal that round's partner actions in advance. Report seed-level results and uncertainty; a null or reversed partner change leaves the intended withdrawal test inconclusive.

cases.question: Can agents coordinate a product launch with task dependencies?

design.title: Coordinating a product launch with task dependencies
design.question: Can six model-controlled agents complete a product-launch task graph within 10 rounds, and does communication improve completion while reducing duplicated and blocked work?
design.hypothesis: With the same task graph and matched seeds, communication will increase completion_rate and reduce duplicate_work_rate and blocked_work_rate relative to no communication.
design.context: Agents share a simulated product-launch project. Success is completion of all declared tasks by round 10; completion_rate also captures partial success. The graph has parallel workstreams that converge at launch. Compare outcomes within matched seeds and report variation across seeds, rather than treating a successful run as guaranteed capability. Role labels describe responsibilities, not exclusive task permissions. Launch activities are abstract work packages: no software is deployed, customers contacted, or market outcomes simulated.

design.question: Do six model-controlled agents assigned complementary specialist roles achieve higher task completion than six generalists on the same dependency-constrained project?
design.hypothesis: Specialist role assignments increase completion_rate and reduce duplicate_work_rate; blocked_work_rate may increase if specialization creates handoff bottlenecks.
design.context: The team completes two parallel workstreams, A and B. Each has research, design, implementation, review, testing and integration work packages. output.explanation: This can be tested, but no run results were supplied, so consistency cannot yet be determined. design.title: Cross-seed robustness of cooperation under scarcity
design.question: Does the effect of scarce versus abundant resources on model-controlled agents’ contribution rates have a consistent direction across random seeds?
design.hypothesis: Scarcity changes contribution rates in a direction that is reproducible across seeds; the direction is not assumed in advance.
design.context: Use the supplied commons study. Cooperation is operationalized as the fraction of available resources contributed, not the absolute contribution. For each seed and repetition, average contribution_rate across all six agents and 12 rounds in each condition, then subtract abundant from scarce. Average the two paired differences within each seed. Define directional consistency as at least five of six seed-level differences having the same strictly positive or strictly negative sign; zeros do not count toward either direction. Report all seed-level differences, their range, the mean paired difference, and whether the two repetitions agree in sign within each seed. Treat this threshold as descriptive robustness, not proof of a universal effect. Agents and rounds within a run are not independent replications.

design.title: Which agent pairs develop reciprocal exchange?
design.question: Which observed agent pairs show repeated positive transfers and returns, and does episodic memory change the emergence of these patterns?
design.hypothesis: Episodic memory will support more persistent reciprocal exchanges in some pairs than no retained history. With identical agent goals, specific pair identities are exploratory rather than predicted.
design.context: Use the environment's existing paired-transfer mechanics and pairing schedule; do not assume partner choice or impose new matching rules. Analyze trust_rate and return_rate by observed pair, condition and seed. Operationally flag a reciprocal pattern when positive transfers receive positive returns on at least three observed exchanges within a pair. Describe a pattern as developing only when both rates are higher in rounds 7–12 than in rounds 1–6, with at least two exchange opportunities in each window. Report opportunity counts and insufficient exposure rather than treating unobserved exchanges as zero. These descriptive thresholds do not establish motives. Compare the same pair labels across matched-seed conditions, but assess consistency across independent seeds rather than treating pair labels as stable personalities.

cases.question: Does a larger public-good multiplier reduce free riding?

design.title: Public-good multipliers and free riding
design.question: Does increasing the public-good multiplier from 2 to 4 increase model-controlled agents' contribution rate, holding endowments and other settings constant?
design.hypothesis: The higher multiplier increases average contribution rate, reducing the operational free-riding index defined as one minus contribution rate.
design.context: Six model-controlled agents make sealed contributions and receive shared returns under the commons rules. Compare multipliers of 2 and 4 with otherwise identical settings and profiles. Treat each seed's complete group trajectory as the independent experimental unit. For each seed, average contribution_rate across agents and rounds, then calculate the high-minus-low multiplier difference. Report all three paired differences and their mean and range; do not treat agents or rounds as independent replicates. Define the free-riding index as 1 minus contribution_rate; it describes withheld contributions, not intent. Group payoff is secondary because changing the multiplier directly changes returns.
